title: Linux OOM Killer Invocation Tracking
exclusions: Detects collected Linux kernel invocation headers containing `invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=... order=...`; it does not require or parse a victim record. UC-1.1.7 separately detects `Killed process ... total-vm:` victim records. This UC does not prove that the invoking task exhausted memory, identify the selected victim, determine host-wide versus memory-cgroup scope from the invocation line alone, reconstruct a multiline OOM sequence, detect userspace allocation failures, or cover kernel records retained only in an uncollected journal or ring buffer. It does not remediate memory pressure or provide regulatory attestation.
evidence: After deployment, retain the `UC-1.1.131 - Linux OOM Killer Invocation Tracking` saved-search definition and dispatch history, each matching raw invocation header and parsed result, the effective file-monitor input and add-on version, source-coverage reconciliation, and dated positive and negative control-test outputs. These artifacts document the configured detector and observed invocation records; they do not prove complete host coverage, root cause, or runtime validation by this editorial review.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Apply the SPL pipeline beginning at `rex` to one synthetic event with `host=oom-lab-01` and `_raw="Jul 28 09:00:00 oom-lab-01 kernel: java invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x140cca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE|__GFP_COMP), nodemask=(null), order=0, oom_score_adj=500"`. Expect exactly one row with `invoker_process=java`, `gfp_mask=0x140cca`, `gfp_flags=GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE|__GFP_COMP`, `node_mask=(null)`, `allocation_order=0`, `adjustment_field=oom_score_adj`, and `oom_adjustment=500`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Apply the same parser and post-processing to one victim-only event with `host=oom-lab-02` and `_raw="Jul 28 09:05:00 oom-lab-02 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process 4242 (java) total-vm:2097152kB, anon-rss:1048576kB, file-rss:4096kB, shmem-rss:0kB"`. Expect zero rows because a victim record is UC-1.1.7's signal and does not contain an OOM invocation header.

dataSources: Linux kernel messages persisted to the active text system log, commonly `/var/log/messages` and distribution-dependently `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/kern.log`, collected by a Universal Forwarder file monitor managed with the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833). Assign Splunk's pretrained `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog` and the locally selected `index=os`. Required indexed fields are `_time`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`; the SPL derives `invoker_process`, `gfp_mask`, `gfp_flags`, `node_mask`, `allocation_order`, `adjustment_field`, `adjustment_semantics`, and `oom_adjustment`.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) for managed file collection. `linux_messages_syslog` is a pretrained Splunk platform source type, not an add-on-specific OOM input.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog "kernel:" "invoked oom-killer:" "gfp_mask=" earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| rex field=_raw "(?i)kernel(?:\[\d+\])?:\s*(?:\[[^\]\r\n]+\]\s*)?(?<invoker_process>.+?)\s+invoked oom-killer:\s+gfp_mask=(?<gfp_mask>0x[0-9a-f]+)(?:\((?<gfp_flags>[^)\r\n]+)\))?(?:,\s+nodemask=(?<node_mask>[^,\r\n]+))?,\s+order=(?<allocation_order>-?\d+),\s+(?<adjustment_field>oom_score_adj|oomkilladj)=(?<oom_adjustment>-?\d+)"
| where isnotnull(invoker_process) AND isnotnull(gfp_mask) AND isnotnull(allocation_order) AND isnotnull(oom_adjustment)
| eval gfp_flags=coalesce(gfp_flags,"not_logged"), node_mask=coalesce(node_mask,"not_logged"), adjustment_semantics=if(adjustment_field="oomkilladj","legacy_oomkilladj","oom_score_adj")
| table _time host invoker_process gfp_mask gfp_flags node_mask allocation_order adjustment_semantics oom_adjustment source
| sort 0 -_time
description: Reports one row for each collected Linux kernel OOM invocation header and extracts the task that made the failing allocation plus the kernel-reported allocation context. The scheduled search evaluates one completed five-minute event-time window and fires when at least one complete `invoked oom-killer` header parses; it intentionally does not count victim-only records.
value: The invocation header can survive when no standard victim line is present, when the kernel is configured to panic, or when the later sequence is truncated. Capturing the allocating task, GFP mask, allocation order, and OOM adjustment gives Linux and workload owners earlier, more precise evidence for capacity triage while avoiding the false claim that the invoker was necessarily the victim or cause.
implementation: Collect the distro-specific text log that receives kernel messages with a Universal Forwarder managed by `Splunk_TA_nix`, assign `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog`, and route it to the locally chosen `os` index. Validate the modern and legacy invocation formats, then schedule the search every five minutes over `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`; trigger when the result count is greater than zero. Use adjacent kernel context for cgroup and victim analysis rather than joining separate lines in the alert SPL.
visualization: Use a 24-hour single value for parsed invocations, a timechart split by `host`, and a detail table containing `_time`, `host`, `invoker_process`, `gfp_mask`, `gfp_flags`, `node_mask`, `allocation_order`, `adjustment_semantics`, `oom_adjustment`, and `source`. Add drilldowns to the same host's raw kernel records for ±30 seconds and to validated memory telemetry; never label the invoker as the killed process.
dataModelAcceleration: No standard CIM dataset represents a Linux kernel OOM invocation header with these source-specific allocation fields. Keep the raw-event SPL; do not claim a `tstats` equivalent or enable acceleration solely for this use case.

knownFalsePositives:
The parsed signature is evidence that the kernel printed an OOM invocation header; the cases below are authorized or operationally expected invocations, not fabricated events.

1. **Approved stress-ng or Magic SysRq `f` resilience test** — A controlled fault-injection exercise can deliberately invoke the OOM killer. Match the exact lab host, owner, command or SysRq action, and change window before downgrading the page; preserve the invocation as test evidence.

2. **Kubernetes or Red Hat OpenShift memory-cgroup limit** — A pod can exhaust its cgroup while the node still has free memory. Inspect the adjacent `oom-kill:constraint=...` or older `Task in ... killed as a result of limit of ...` records, then correlate the cgroup path with pod UID, container status, configured limit, and orchestrator events. Route an approved batch eviction to the workload owner; do not suppress every invocation on the node.

3. **systemd `MemoryMax=` enforcement** — A service intentionally capped by its unit can trigger an OOM invocation. Confirm the adjacent cgroup context and `systemctl show <unit> -p MemoryMax,MemoryCurrent,Result`; repeated invocations remain a capacity or configuration defect unless a dated test authorizes them.

4. **Slurm or other HPC job limit** — A batch job may exceed an assigned memory boundary and be disposable by policy. Correlate host, `invoker_process`, cgroup or job ID, allocation, and scheduler completion state; suppress only the approved job class and time window.

5. **Duplicate local and relay collection** — The same invocation can arrive from a local file monitor and a central syslog relay. Compare `_raw`, `_time`, `host`, and `source`, then remove the overlapping input. Do not add broad `dedup`, because genuine invocations can repeat with identical allocation fields.

If notification suppression is permitted, use a reviewed `linux_oom_invocation_exceptions.csv` lookup with exact `host`, `invoker_process`, UTC `start_epoch`, UTC `end_epoch`, `owner`, and `reason`. Apply it after parsing, preserve suppressed rows in a review report, reject wildcards and non-expiring entries, and never suppress solely because the event came from a container host. The base SPL intentionally contains no lookup.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal semantics

Install a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) on the Linux Universal Forwarders used for collection and on any Splunk tiers required by the deployment topology. The Splunkbase compatibility listing retrieved during this documentation review includes Splunk platform 9.2 and later, but no platform/add-on combination was run here. Verify the current compatibility matrix and test add-on changes outside production. Give the forwarder service account read access to the selected system-log file and normal outbound access to the receiving tier. Give the monitoring role read access to the operating-system index plus permission to create and schedule the saved search.

Identify the one durable text log that actually receives kernel messages on every in-scope distribution. Typical paths are `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/syslog`, and `/var/log/kern.log`; verify the active path instead of enabling all three. This implementation does not poll `dmesg`. The kernel ring buffer can wrap, and `dmesg` output is a diagnostic view rather than the primary indexed source. If a host stores kernel records only in the systemd journal, establish an approved journal-to-text or remote-syslog collection path first, or record that host as uncovered.

The Linux kernel's current `dump_header()` source prints the allocating task followed by `invoked oom-killer`, a hexadecimal GFP allocation mask, optional decoded GFP flags, allocation order, and `oom_score_adj`. Older Red Hat examples use the legacy field name `oomkilladj`, and some supported records omit decoded flags and `nodemask`. The invocation identifies the task in whose allocation path the kernel entered OOM handling. It does not establish that this task consumed the memory, was selected as the victim, or was killed. The kernel's default `oom_kill_allocating_task=0` behavior explicitly allows another task to be selected. UC-1.1.7 covers the later victim signature and is intentionally different.

Modern kernels can print a separate `oom-kill:constraint=...` context line with cgroup and victim information. Older kernels may print `Task in <cgroup> killed as a result of limit of <cgroup>`. Because these are separate events and syslog timestamps can have only one-second precision, the production SPL does not join them to an invocation header by time. Such a join can cross-associate concurrent OOM sequences. Operators retrieve the surrounding raw sequence in the drilldown and determine scope from the actual context line.

## Step 1 — Configure and verify collection

Use a Universal Forwarder file monitor managed with `Splunk_TA_nix`; do not create a generic HEC token, API poll, or recurring `dmesg` scripted input for this detector. Splunk documents that Universal Forwarders enable add-on inputs through configuration files and that only the stanzas being changed should be copied to `local/inputs.conf`. Select one non-overlapping monitor for the verified kernel-bearing file, route it to the locally approved event index, and assign Splunk's pretrained `linux_messages_syslog` source type. For a verified Red Hat-style host, a dedicated stanza can take this form:

```ini
[monitor:///var/log/messages]
disabled = 0
sourcetype = linux_messages_syslog
index = os
```

Use `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/kern.log` only when it is the verified source. If an add-on-supplied broad `/var/log` stanza already monitors the file, edit the existing local override rather than adding another monitor. `index=os` is a catalogue convention and deployment choice, not a property of the source type; create and secure that index or replace its name consistently in the input and SPL. Do not collect the same file both locally and through a syslog relay.

After deployment, inspect the effective input with `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and the forwarder's input status. Run this coverage search:

```spl
index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog earliest=-24h
| stats count min(_time) AS first_event max(_time) AS last_event values(source) AS sources by host
```

Reconcile the returned hosts against the in-scope Linux inventory and confirm each `source` is the intended current file. On one representative host per distribution and kernel family, compare a harmless recent kernel line from `journalctl -k` or the persisted file with its Splunk `_time`, `host`, `source`, and raw text. This comparison verifies transport without inducing memory exhaustion. Measure `_indextime-_time` for the source so the scheduled delay is based on observed ingestion latency.

Expected event volume for this signature is zero during healthy operation. A steady stream is an incident or a deliberately authorized stress test, not an input heartbeat. Maintain a separate source-coverage alert because zero OOM results cannot distinguish healthy hosts from silent forwarders.

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Save the catalogue SPL as `UC-1.1.131 - Linux OOM Killer Invocation Tracking`. Schedule it with cron `*/5 * * * *`. Its embedded `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` searches the completed five-minute event-time bucket immediately before the latest bucket and permits five minutes for routine indexing delay. Trigger when the number of results is greater than zero. The threshold is one parsed invocation header in the completed window; it is not a memory-percentage or rate threshold.

```spl
index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog "kernel:" "invoked oom-killer:" "gfp_mask=" earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| rex field=_raw "(?i)kernel(?:\[\d+\])?:\s*(?:\[[^\]\r\n]+\]\s*)?(?<invoker_process>.+?)\s+invoked oom-killer:\s+gfp_mask=(?<gfp_mask>0x[0-9a-f]+)(?:\((?<gfp_flags>[^)\r\n]+)\))?(?:,\s+nodemask=(?<node_mask>[^,\r\n]+))?,\s+order=(?<allocation_order>-?\d+),\s+(?<adjustment_field>oom_score_adj|oomkilladj)=(?<oom_adjustment>-?\d+)"
| where isnotnull(invoker_process) AND isnotnull(gfp_mask) AND isnotnull(allocation_order) AND isnotnull(oom_adjustment)
| eval gfp_flags=coalesce(gfp_flags,"not_logged"), node_mask=coalesce(node_mask,"not_logged"), adjustment_semantics=if(adjustment_field="oomkilladj","legacy_oomkilladj","oom_score_adj")
| table _time host invoker_process gfp_mask gfp_flags node_mask allocation_order adjustment_semantics oom_adjustment source
| sort 0 -_time
```

### Understanding this SPL

The base search fixes the configured event index and Splunk's documented Linux system-message source type, then requires the syslog `kernel:` marker and the stable invocation tokens. It does not use broad `Out of memory`, `oom-kill`, or `Killed process` alternatives, so UC-1.1.7 victim rows and unrelated application messages do not satisfy this detector.

`rex` begins after the kernel program marker and tolerates an optional bracketed kernel timestamp before capturing `invoker_process`. It extracts the hexadecimal GFP mask, an optional parenthesized flag rendering, an optional NUMA node mask, the allocation order, and either the current `oom_score_adj` or legacy `oomkilladj` name. `where` rejects truncated headers and format variants missing the required values rather than producing a misleading partial alert. `eval` labels omitted optional fields as `not_logged` and preserves whether the adjustment used modern or legacy semantics. `table` retains `source` for provenance, and `sort` presents newest invocations first.

Do not translate `gfp_mask` into a guessed business severity. It describes the allocation request's kernel flags; symbolic text is kernel-version dependent. Allocation order zero requests one base page, while higher orders request contiguous powers-of-two pages, but a high order does not by itself establish exhausted total RAM. `oom_score_adj` affects victim selection; it does not measure memory consumed. The invoker and the eventual victim can differ. Keep these facts in dashboard labels and analyst notes.

No CIM model supplies this event schema. Host-memory metrics from a validated `vmstat` or other metric source are useful drilldowns, but they are not required to detect the invocation header and do not justify a fictitious Performance data-model mapping.

## Step 3 — Validate parser, scheduling, and scope boundaries

Use an isolated `| makeresults` search to set `_raw` and `host` to the exact positive value in `controlTest`, then append the production pipeline beginning at `rex`. It must return one row with `invoker_process=java`, `gfp_mask=0x140cca`, decoded flags, `node_mask=(null)`, order `0`, modern adjustment semantics, and value `500`. Repeat with the negative victim-only event; it must return no rows. This negative is important: the event is a real OOM kill, but it belongs to UC-1.1.7 rather than this invocation detector.

Also test a documented legacy header such as `kernel: httpd invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x201d2, order=0, oomkilladj=0`. It should produce one row with `gfp_flags=not_logged`, `node_mask=not_logged`, `adjustment_semantics=legacy_oomkilladj`, and `oom_adjustment=0`. Test one intentionally truncated line without `order`; it must produce zero rows. Retain these parser controls whenever the regular expression changes.

For end-to-end collection validation, obtain an existing OOM sequence from an approved non-production host or a vendor incident sample and preserve the raw events in order. Compare the invocation header in the persisted file with the indexed event and parsed saved-search row. For Linux, there is no vendor OOM dashboard; compare with the native journal interface (`journalctl -k`) and the persisted system-log file for the same host and time. Use the same-host ±30-second raw-event drilldown to locate `oom-kill:constraint=...`, memory-cgroup limit text, panic text, and any victim record. Confirm that the Splunk table calls the parsed task the invoker, not the killed process. Do not induce an OOM on production. If an operations owner authorizes `stress-ng` or Magic SysRq `f`, confine it to an expendable lab host with a change record, console access, and an explicit recovery plan.

Check dispatch history after two cycles. Consecutive jobs should cover adjacent completed five-minute windows without gaps. Compare `_time` and `_indextime` on representative kernel records; if routine latency exceeds five minutes, increase the delay while retaining closed, non-overlapping windows. Validate daily source coverage against the Linux inventory independently of OOM results.

These validation steps are implementation instructions. During this editorial review, no event was ingested, no kernel OOM was induced, and no SPL was executed on Splunk. Keep `status=draft` until the parser and collection path are validated in a supported deployment and reviewed by an accountable Linux/Splunk owner.

## Step 4 — Operationalize, investigate, and retain evidence

Build a dashboard with a 24-hour invocation count, a timechart by host, and a raw result table using the fields in `visualization`. Set a drilldown to `index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog host=<selected-host> earliest=<event-time-30s> latest=<event-time+30s>` and display events in ascending time order. This surrounding sequence is where modern `constraint`, `oom_memcg`, `task_memcg`, selected task, PID, UID, memory state, and victim records can be assessed without an unsafe timestamp join in the alert.

Route every new production invocation to Linux operations. Add the workload owner when the adjacent cgroup path or service inventory identifies one. Escalate immediately when critical service impact, repeated host-wide invocations, `panic_on_oom`, or no killable process is reported. Do not automatically add memory, restart services, alter cgroup limits, change `vm.panic_on_oom`, or kill processes from this alert.

The response runbook should verify the raw signature, identify the invoker and its allocation context, then inspect the full same-host OOM sequence. Determine whether the constraint is global, cpuset, mempolicy, or memory cgroup from the context line—not from the invocation header. Identify the selected victim separately, assess service impact and restart behavior, compare memory and swap telemetry before the event, and review deployments or limit changes. The invoker may simply be the task whose allocation encountered the condition; call it the root cause only when independent evidence supports that conclusion.

Process and cgroup names can expose workload or tenant details. Restrict raw-event and dashboard access under the operational-log policy. For every deployment or parser revision, retain the saved-search export, owner, exact time bounds, alert and dispatch history, raw and parsed control samples, effective `inputs.conf`, add-on version, inventory reconciliation, measured ingestion latency, reviewer, and change ticket. Follow local retention policy; do not claim this operational evidence alone certifies regulatory compliance.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

- **No kernel events appear for the host:** check whether the machine is journal-only, whether the selected file receives kernel messages, whether the forwarder account can read it, and whether the event was routed to `index=os` with `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog`. Restore source coverage before interpreting zero OOM rows as health.
- **The host reports OOM activity but this search has no row:** first distinguish an invocation header from a victim-only record. UC-1.1.7 should detect `Killed process ... total-vm:` even when this UC has no match. If an invocation exists, confirm its file, index, source type, `kernel:` marker, `_indextime`, and whether line truncation removed `order` or the adjustment field.
- **The raw header is present but fields are null:** compare the event with modern and legacy primary-source formats. Look for a journald transport that removed the `kernel:` program marker, an unexpected process prefix, uppercase field names, or a kernel/vendor format not represented by the controls. Preserve the sample and extend the expression only with paired positive and negative tests.
- **The invoker is mistaken for the victim:** retrieve the later `oom-kill:constraint` and `Killed process` records. Rename any local dashboard column that says `process` to `invoker_process`; use UC-1.1.7 for victim fields.
- **Cgroup scope is missing:** this is expected in the primary row. Scope is not carried in the invocation header on the documented formats. Inspect adjacent same-host records; do not infer memory-cgroup scope from `invoker_process`, `node_mask`, or an orchestrator host label.
- **Rows are duplicated:** compare `_raw`, `_time`, `host`, and `source`, then remove overlap between a local monitor, broad `/var/log` monitor, and syslog relay. Do not hide input topology defects with `dedup`.
- **The host field names the relay:** sender identity was lost at ingestion. Correct host attribution in the validated syslog input/parser; do not rewrite `host` in this search from an unverified raw token.
- **The alert arrives one bucket late:** compare `_time`, `_indextime`, NTP state, file flush behavior, and forwarder queues. Change the dispatch delay from measured latency while preserving non-overlapping closed windows.
- **Expected cgroup tests page the on-call:** use the exact, expiring lookup process in `knownFalsePositives` only after field extraction. Preserve all suppressed records for review and never create a permanent host-wide exception.
grandmaExplanation: We catch the moment Linux says it has run out of usable memory and is starting its emergency response. That early clue helps people investigate before mistaking the program that noticed the problem for the program that caused it.
